title: The four elements
hook: hardness, fluid, heat, motion: the body as four. but are the four real?
tomorrow: which four thoughts could go out the door with you every morning?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one meal followed all the way from the village to the body, so the craving loosens. Food's journey. Today the body the food becomes.

What is your body actually made of? A chemistry class hands you a chart of elements. Buddhaghosa hands you four, and they aren't chemistry. They're things you can feel from the inside, right now: something hard, something fluid, something warm, something moving. Earth, water, fire, air. The practice is to look at the body as only that. And Buddhist thinkers have disagreed over one question: are the four themselves real?
screen: `A CHART, OR FOUR?` → `HARD, FLUID, WARM, MOVING.` → `ARE THE FOUR REAL?`

segments.voice: It starts with the Buddha's advice to his son Rahula. Whatever in you is hard and solid, hair, nails, teeth, bones, is the earth element. Whatever is fluid, blood, sweat, tears, is water. Whatever warms you and digests your food is fire. Whatever moves, the breath going in and out, is air. And each one, he says, is to be seen as it is: this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Buddhaghosa turns it into a meditation subject, with a short method for quick minds and a long one for the rest of us. Now the two views. In the Theravada Abhidhamma, the analysis bottoms out in basic qualities like these: hardness is really there when you press your palm down, and seeing it plainly is what loosens the grip of me. Nagarjuna, the Mahayana philosopher, examines the elements in his Middle Way verses, takes space as his example, and says the others go the same way: none has a fixed being of its own. Even earth is only earth next to what it isn't. Each side has a strong case. One says you need something solid to stand on while you let go. The other says that if you grip the four as things, you've only traded one self for four.
screen: `THE BUDDHA'S ADVICE TO RAHULA.` · `NOT MINE, NOT ME, NOT MY SELF.` · `ABHIDHAMMA: THE QUALITIES ARE REAL.` · `NAGARJUNA: NONE HAS A FIXED BEING.` · then, large: `FOUR ELEMENTS.`

segments.voice: Press one palm against your leg and feel the hardness: earth. Notice the wet of your mouth: water. The warmth where your hands rest: fire. The breath moving in and out: air. Go round the four slowly, naming each one under your breath.
The four elements: earth, water, fire, air, felt as hardness, fluid, warmth and motion. Rahula heard them first, from his father.
Pocket this one: four elements, and not one of them signed with your name. Thirty-eight of forty.

howItsDone: In Theravada practice the defining of the four elements is a meditation subject in the Visuddhimagga, done by a brief or a detailed method; Mahayana students meet the elements again in Nagarjuna's analysis of emptiness.

fork.setup: your friend says the Abhidhamma view is naive: "hardness is just a word." give the Abhidhamma side its best case.
options: it's settled because an old book says so.
hardness is felt, not invented; you need something real to see.
it was the best science anyone had back then.
fork.reveal: its strongest point: the hardness under your palm is there whether you name it or not, and seeing it plainly loosens the grip of me. Nagarjuna's side answers that gripping the four as things just trades one self for four.

chat.says: hand cramped all shift from the mat cutter. ông said "just earth, water, fire, wind." comforting or creepy?
options: Comforting, mostly: seeing the parts plainly loosens the grip of my pain, my body.
Creepy. It means your body isn't real, so the pain doesn't actually matter.
Neither. It's poetry: how people described anatomy before real science came.
chat.meaning: The Buddha told Rahula to see each element as it is: not mine, not me. The pain is real; the grip loosens.

tie.story: The Buddha told Rahula to see hardness, fluid, warmth and motion as not mine.
tie.friend: Mai's sore hand is real, and seeing it as four plain qualities can loosen the grip.
tie.you: which of the four can you feel most clearly right now?

Rahula.meaning: the Buddha's son, who later became a monk

Abhidhamma.meaning: the part of the Pali canon that analyzes mind and matter

Nagarjuna.meaning: a Mahayana philosopher who taught that nothing has a fixed being

Theravada.meaning: the Buddhism of Sri Lanka, Thailand, Laos and Myanmar

Mahayana.meaning: the Buddhism of Vietnam, China, Korea, Japan and Tibet

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 62, Maharahulovada Sutta (the earth, water, fire and air elements within: hair, nails, teeth, bones; bile, blood, sweat, tears; what warms and digests; the in-breath and out-breath; each to be seen as it is: this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self)
Visuddhimagga 11 (the defining of the four elements: the brief method for those of quick understanding and the detailed method)
Mulamadhyamakakarika 5 (examination of the elements: space taken as the example; the remaining elements treated in the same way)

notes: MN 62, Visuddhimagga 11 and MMK 5 paraphrased. Confirm the examples chosen from MN 62's lists and the summary of the two methods in Vism 11.

A scholar should confirm the one-line summaries are fair to both, and the line 'even earth is only earth next to what it isn't' as a gloss on MMK 5's argument that a characteristic and the characterized depend on each other.
